These findings suggest a context-dependent role of central arousal in pain modulation: high catastrophizing with strong autonomic reactivity may characterize a subgroup with less efficient endogenous analgesia. Pupillary reactivity to a cold pressor test did not predict conditioned pain modulation on its own, but pain catastrophizing was associated with less efficient pressure pain inhibition mainly in participants with greater pupillary reactivity. Central arousal, to which the locus coeruleus-noradrenergic system contributes, may therefore act as a context-dependent gate rather than a uniformly antinociceptive mechanism. Combining an objective autonomic marker with a brief cognitive measure may help identify individuals at risk of less efficient endogenous analgesia.

title: Learning points for nephrologists from the 2026 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Guidelines for the management of cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease, developed in collaboration with the ERA.
journal: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association
abstract: The brand new '2026 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease, developed in collaboration with the ERA' are the first European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Guidelines to consider management of both cardiovascular disease (CVD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD), and are unique in their breadth and depth of considerations on the topic. Updated ESC methodology is employed to assess the levels of evidence that support 165 formally structured recommendation statements. These are accompanied by practical treatment algorithms. A key objective was to encourage screening for CKD and basic management of risk of CVD and kidney failure by all clinicians who encounter patients with CKD, with the aim of reducing global disease burden. The full version of the guidelines is reproduced in Nephrology Dialysis Transplantation, and this accompanying report is a synopsis of key learning points for the nephrology community. We particularly highlight when the presence of CKD modifies standard approaches to CVD management. Special consideration is given to practical pre-transplant CVD assessment and avoidance of contrast-induced acute kidney injury without delaying procedures or interventions. The guidance should assist in planning health services to ensure this high-risk patient group with CVD and CKD are managed effectively without prejudice or delay despite potential complexities of co-existent CKD. This synopsis also highlights areas of contention where better evidence is needed and includes a comparison of key points between the 2026 ESC Guidelines and the KDIGO (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes) 2024 guideline for the evaluation and management of CKD.

title: Eupatilin Mitigates the Neuropathology Induced by Aβ Oligomers/NMDA.
abstract: Eupatilin, a flavonoid derivative, can be extracted from many plants including Artemisia argyi, Artemisia princeps, and Salvia plebeia. Using a screening platform, we have previously found that eupatilin mitigates the abnormal depolarization brought about by Aβ oligomers. Our aim was to explore in detail how eupatilin affects the mechanisms involved in neuronal functioning and thence animal behavior. We implemented a study involving both mice primary glutamatergic neurons and the J20 Alzheimer's disease (AD) mouse model. Cellular and molecular mechanisms were investigated using a membrane potential sensitive dye DiBAC4(3), Fura2/AM calcium influx measurement, and Western blotting. The efficacy on behavior was tested using Novel Object Recognition and the Morris Water Maze. Eupatilin inhibits Aβ oligomers-induced neuronal depolarization at a low concentration. Furthermore, eupatilin effectively blocks NMDA-induced, but not AMPA-induced depolarization, which indicates its specificity. Eupatilin was also able to suppress both Aβ oligomer-induced and NMDA-induced increases in ERK phosphorylation. In addition, eupatilin prevents both Aβ oligomer-induced influx and NMDA-induced calcium influx in neurons. The steady state calcium influx caused by NMDA is immediately reduced by the addition of eupatilin. Finally, eupatilin is capable of alleviating impairment to novel object recognition and spatial learning/memory present in the J20 mice. Aβ oligomers-induced pathophysiology can be mitigated by the pure natural compound eupatilin. This compound has an excellent chance of being developed into a therapeutic drug for AD.

title: Can Strengthening Stress Resilience Slow Biological Aging? A Hypothesis-Generating Framework for Study Design, Measurement Harmonization, and Intervention Development.
abstract: Prolonged psychological stress has been associated with accelerated biological aging, but the possibility that strengthening stress resilience may slow biological aging remains largely untested. This gap reflects the rare pre-specification of resilience and biological aging endpoints within the same trial, the separate development of resilience neuroscience instruments and geroscience biomarker panels, and the infrequent evaluation of stress-related interventions against biological aging outcomes. In this hypothesis-generating narrative review, we propose a framework that treats three neurobehavioral systems implicated in stress resilience-hippocampal pattern separation, prefrontal cognitive control, and reward-system engagement-as candidate targets. The design pillar pairs an outcome-based resilience measure with a pre-specified hierarchy of biological aging endpoints, led by DunedinPACE, and links four working hypotheses to explicit estimands. The harmonization pillar specifies a minimum core measurement set collected in the same participants at matched time points. In the intervention pillar, psychological, social, and pharmacological programs test the target engagement hypothesis and document the engagement of their neurobehavioral target, so that changes in biological aging markers can be examined in relation to the targeted system. The proposed approach can generate falsifiable predictions on whether strengthening resilience may slow biological aging in humans, a necessary step before the effects on healthspan or lifespan can be examined.

title: Compartment-Specific Citrate Uncoupling as a Metabolic-Epigenetic Driver of Neurodegeneration: A Dual-Axis Hypothesis with Transcriptomic Evidence from GSE5281 and SEA-AD.
abstract: Prevailing models of neurodegeneration center on amyloid-β and tau, yet metabolic dysfunction precedes proteinopathy by decades. We propose compartment-specific citrate uncoupling: opposing disturbances of citrate in neurons and astrocytes as a proteinopathy-independent driver of neurodegeneration. In neurons, a Warburg-like shift depletes cytosolic citrate, which starves ATP-citrate lyase (ACLY) and erodes the H3K27ac/H3K9ac marks that sustain synaptic gene expression, while loss of citrate-mediated PFK1 inhibition collapses the SLC13A5-dependent glycolytic gate. In surviving astrocytes, loss of ACO1, with SLC13A3 a weaker and less specific accompaniment, traps newly synthesized citrate intracellularly; ACLY then hyper-activates and STAT3 hyperacetylation drives an A1 identity. The intercellular citrate gradient inverts. We reanalyzed GSE5281 (161 postmortem samples across six brain regions). Core TCA-cycle enzymes were coherently downregulated in Alzheimer's disease in five of six regions, more strongly in women, and not in the disease-spared visual cortex. The SLC13 transporter family instead shifted in opposite directions across regions. A cell-type-resolved reanalysis of the SEA-AD multiregion atlas placed the astrocytic arm on ACO1, which fell with pseudo-progression in all nine regions tested; SLC13A3 fell across most cortical cell types and is not compartment-specific. A four-proposition framework then combines PDK1 induction, Cryo-NanoSIMS, MALDI-TIMS-MSI, and spatial transcriptomics. If the model holds, neurodegeneration reads as a routing failure of a central metabolic hub.

title: The Placental Epigenome in Preterm Birth: From Cellular Heterogeneity to Liquid Biopsy Biomarkers.
abstract: Preterm birth (PTB) remains a leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality worldwide, with limited tools for early prediction or targeted prevention. Increasing evidence identifies the placenta as a central regulator of gestational duration, and alterations in placental gene regulatory programs have been associated with PTB. This review synthesizes recent advances in placental genomics and epigenomics, emphasizing how cell-type-specific regulatory landscapes shape PTB risk. We describe how DNA methylation, chromatin accessibility, and transcriptional heterogeneity across trophoblasts, Hofbauer cells, endothelial cells, Natural Killer (NK) cells, and mesenchymal stromal cells integrate maternal, fetal, immune, and environmental signals. We further evaluate emerging liquid biopsy approaches, focusing on circulating cell-free placental DNA (cfpDNA) methylation as a minimally invasive strategy to detect placental dysfunction. Single-cell and long-read sequencing technologies have enabled high-resolution mapping of placental regulatory architecture, revealing cell-type-specific pathways underlying inflammation, impaired trophoblast differentiation, and aberrant vascular remodeling. These studies support the investigation of placental epigenetic alterations as potential contributors to PTB-associated biology, although their causal roles and consistency across PTB subtypes remain uncertain. Circulating cfpDNA methylation profiles are being investigated as minimally invasive indicators of placental biology, but their accuracy and clinical utility for PTB prediction require further validation. Together, these findings suggest that epigenomic alterations may be associated with biological pathways implicated in PTB and may also provide measurable molecular signatures in maternal circulation.

title: What Radiomics Teaches Us About Vestibular Schwannoma Biology: Imaging Biomarkers, Artificial Intelligence, and Future Clinical Translation: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Background/Objective: Vestibular schwannoma is a benign Schwann cell tumor characterized by marked biological and clinical heterogeneity, resulting in highly variable growth patterns, hearing outcomes and treatment responses. Advances in molecular biology have improved the understanding of the pathways driving tumor development, highlighting the roles of NF2-related signaling, angiogenesis, inflammation and tumor-microenvironment interactions. In parallel, quantitative imaging, radiomics, and artificial intelligence (AI) are being investigated for tumor characterization and outcome prediction, although the biological specificity of many imaging-derived features remains unproven. Methods: This narrative review was conducted by examining recent literature on the role of radiomics in Vestibular schwannoma biology. Results: Across published studies reviewed we summarize the current knowledge on vestibular schwannoma biology and discusses the clinical potential of quantitative MRI, volumetric analysis, radiomics and AI for tumor characterization, growth prediction, treatment-response assessment, automated segmentation and functional outcome prediction. Conclusions: Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing reported predictive associations from validated biological correlates and on the potential value of integrating imaging with molecular data. Finally, current limitations, including methodological heterogeneity, lack of standardization and the need for multicenter validation, are discussed to outline future directions for clinical translation.

title: Transcriptomic and Metabolomic Remodeling of the Cockroach Brain Following Envenomation by Parasitoid Wasp Ampulex compressa.
abstract: The parasitoid jewel wasp Ampulex compressa induces prolonged hypokinesia in its cockroach host, Periplaneta americana, by injecting venom into the central nervous system. Although acute behavioral effects are well characterized, molecular processes associated with persistent hypokinesia remain poorly understood. We combined transcriptomics and untargeted metabolomics to characterize brain changes 24 h after envenomation. RNA-seq of the central brain region containing the central complex and adjacent tissue identified 331 differentially expressed genes: 267 upregulated and 64 downregulated. Increased expression of tyrosine decarboxylase-like and arrestin-domain genes, together with reduced expression of a putative tyramine/octopamine receptor, suggests altered regulation of aminergic signaling. Changes in synaptic vesicle and innexin transcripts further implicate chemical and electrical synaptic function. Immune, detoxification, and extracellular-matrix genes were also affected. Independent metabolomic analyses revealed significant increases in fumaric acid and sorbitol, consistent with altered energy metabolism. Tyramine, octopamine, glutamate, and GABA showed no significant differences after multiple-testing correction, although several showed greater inter-individual variation in stung cockroaches. Together, these findings identify changes in neuromodulatory signaling, synaptic organization, and metabolic support as candidate processes associated with persistent hypokinesia. Their contributions to behavioral suppression remain to be distinguished from downstream responses to reduced neural activity and tissue stress.

title: Defining Purity in Botulinum Neurotoxin Type A Formulations: A Narrative Review on Past and Future Developments.
abstract: Botulinum neurotoxin type A (BoNT/A) has become one of the most widely utilized biologics today in both therapeutic and aesthetic applications. Alongside innovative explorations in BoNT/A use, advancements have also been made in manufacturing and formulation practices. The earliest concept of a "pure" BoNT/A referred to the successful isolation of the native neurotoxin complex from Clostridium botulinum, which enabled its clinical development. Subsequently, various definitions of the term "purity" have been applied to BoNT/A, encompassing distinct scientific, regulatory, clinical, and commercial interpretations. Formulation advances first emphasized the removal of non-toxic bacterial components in efforts to reduce protein load and immunogenicity. Increasingly, analytical methods such as SDS-PAGE and ELISA are also commonly cited to support claims for BoNT/A identity and quantity and define purity; however, these provide limited information regarding biological activity. Given that BoNT/A is not a single uniform molecular entity, differences in bacterial strains, manufacturing processes, and the presence or absence of complexing proteins have resulted in distinct product formulations that further complicate direct comparisons relating to purity. This review examines various working definitions of BoNT/A purity, discusses implications for clinicians and patients, and highlights emerging scientific and regulatory efforts to improve product comparability through standardized and biologically relevant measures of potency.

title: OnabotulinumtoxinA Indications and Utilization Among Older Patients with Medicare: A Cross-Sectional Analysis.
abstract: OnabotulinumtoxinA (onabotA) is a neurotoxin that is FDA approved to treat multiple indications. However, data regarding the burden of these indications and onabotA utilization among older adults are limited. This analysis examined the prevalence of onabotA-approved indications and the proportion of those patients treated with onabotA in adults ≥65 years of age in Medicare Fee-for-Service (FFS; 2023) and Medicare Advantage (MA; 2022). Proportions of patients diagnosed with and treated for ≥2 indications were also estimated. Among FFS enrollees, 6.1% of patients were diagnosed with ≥1 indication and 7.0% of diagnosed patients received onabotA. Urological indications (3.2%) and spasticity (2.5%) were most commonly diagnosed, and 80%), and concomitant treatment of these indications was among the lowest (~5%). Differences in diagnosis and onabotA treatment rates by age, sex, and Medicaid eligibility were observed. OnabotA treatment rates among MA enrollees were lower. Among older adults, the most commonly diagnosed onabotA-approved indications had the lowest onabotA treatment rates, suggesting a potential gap between disease burden and real-world treatment utilization.

title: Systematic Review of Algal Toxins in Seals and Sea Lions: Could Unexplained Caspian Seal Mortalities Be Related to Harmful Algae?
abstract: Harmful algal blooms (HABs) produce potent neurotoxins, such as domoic acid (DA) and saxitoxin (STX), which negatively impact marine mammal health. To contextualize these threats within specific regional ecosystems, we conducted a comprehensive meta-analysis of algal toxin concentrations in stranded and non-stranded seals and sea lions reported between 1990 and 2025. Following a systematic screening of 2377 records, 15 studies met the criteria for inclusion in our systematic review and quantitative analysis. Both toxins displayed substantial variability among studies. Notably, the concentrations of DA found in feces were markedly higher than in other matrices, and feces appears to be a high-yield matrix for detecting recent exposure. Urine and serum showed moderate DA levels, while fetal fluids were among the lowest. Geographically, most studies originated from California and the Alaskan Arctic. Multi-matrix monitoring of algal toxins is required in remote or logistically challenging regions. We propose that exposure to algal and cyanobacterial neurotoxins is a testable contributor to recurrent, unexplained mass mortality events among Caspian seals (Pusa caspica) and that targeted toxicological screening within the Caspian Sea ecosystem is urgently needed.

title: Beyond Acute Infection: Long-Term Sequelae of West Nile Virus Disease and the Emerging Concept of "Long WNV".
abstract: West Nile virus (WNV) infection is typically characterized as an acute febrile or neurologic disorder․ Some survivors of WNV develop chronic physical' neurologic' psychological' and functional symptoms lasting months to years․ The extent of illness associated with long-term WNV infection is unknown․ This article reviews published studies of WNV sequelae and mechanisms and evaluates the evidence to support classification of long-term WNV infection as a separate concept' "long WNV". Long-term effects are common among survivors of West Nile fever (WNF) and West Nile neuroinvasive disease and include symptoms such as fatigue' weakness' myalgia' continuing paralysis' problems with mobility and tremors' cognitive difficulties' and depression and other effects on quality of life․ Long-term effects can last for weeks or years․ Proposed causes include continued presence of viral particles' ongoing stimulation of neuroimmune responses' activation of microglial and astrocytic cells' blood-brain barrier dysfunction' complement-mediated synapse loss' neuronal cell death' inhibition of neurogenesis' and immune dysregulation. Accordingly, "Long WNV" is proposed as a provisional descriptive and research concept encompassing persistent, recurrent, or delayed manifestations following WNV infection, rather than an established independent clinical diagnosis. Validated diagnostic criteria and specific biomarkers have not yet been established, and comprehensive longitudinal human studies remain limited. Further longitudinal research combining clinical characterization and other One Health surveillance tools will be important for establishing standard approaches to identifying and treating such conditions․.

title: Fibroblast-IL-7 feedback drives PDPN+ monocytes to restrain CD4+ T cell responses.
abstract: During immune responses, pro- and anti-inflammatory mechanisms must be balanced to ensure pathogen clearance while limiting tissue damage. Monocyte-derived cells contribute to both processes, yet the underlying regulatory circuits remain incompletely defined. Here, we show that a subset of PDPN+IL-7R+ monocyte-derived cells impairs effector CD4+ T cell-mediated control of the intracellular pathogen Leishmania major and thus perpetuates the infection. Fibroblast-derived IL-7 drives this immunosuppressive program, which is upregulated in response to IFNγ. We thus uncover a cytokine-dependent feedback circuit in which elevated IFNγ induces IL-7 production by fibroblasts, licensing immunosuppressive monocyte-derived cells that restrain CD4+ T cell responses. This feedback loop prevents excessive inflammation at the expense of pathogen control and may be targeted to enable therapeutic strategies that enhance antimicrobial immunity while preserving tissue integrity.

title: Clinical Features and Outcomes of Adenovirus Infections in Critically Ill Patients: A Retrospective Multicenter Case-Matched Analysis.
abstract: Human adenovirus (HAdV) infection can lead to severe organ involvement in the ICU, particularly among immunocompromised patients. In this study of ICU patients with HAdV infection, we aimed to 1) determine the prevalence of HAdV disease, 2) identify risk factors for HAdV disease, and 3) evaluate its association with ICU mortality. Retrospective, multicenter, and propensity score case-matched study. Eight ICUs in France. Adult ICU patients admitted between January 2011 and January 2024 with at least one positive HAdV polymerase chain reaction result from any biological sample were included. HAdV infections were classified as either localized infections or systemic HAdV disease. None. A total of 169 patients were analyzed, including 115 patients (68%) classified as localized HAdV infection and 54 patients (32%) as HAdV disease. Hematologic malignancies were significantly more frequent in patients with HAdV disease (74% vs. 37%; p < 0.001). Twenty-three patients (43%) with HAdV disease received allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Pneumonia was the main end-organ manifestation (n = 36/54; 67%). By multivariate analysis, allogeneic HSCT (odds ratio [OR], 3.04) and corticosteroid therapy (OR, 2.89) were independently associated with HAdV disease. ICU mortality was 45% (n = 76). By multivariate analysis, HAdV disease (OR, 3.15), performance status greater than or equal to 2 (OR, 3.35), and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment scores at admission (OR, 1.17 per point) were independently associated with ICU mortality. Mortality remained significantly higher in the HAdV disease group (OR, 10.50) compared with matched ICU patients without HAdV infection. HAdV disease occurred in approximately one-third of ICU patients with HAdV infection, predominantly among those with hematologic malignancies or corticosteroid therapy, and was independently associated with mortality.

title: Neonicotinoids and Mental Health: Mechanistic, Preclinical and Epidemiological Evidence for a Transdiagnostic Neurodevelopmental Risk.
abstract: Neonicotinoid insecticides (imidacloprid, clothianidin, thiacloprid, acetamiprid, thiamethoxam, nitenpyram, dinotefuran) were developed as insect-selective nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) agonists and have long been regarded as safe for vertebrates. However, parent compounds and, more potently, desnitro metabolites such as DN-imidacloprid act on mammalian α4β2 and α7 nAChRs with nicotine-like potency, implicating cholinergic circuits central to cognition, mood, and reward. This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, preclinical, and epidemiological evidence linking neonicotinoid exposure to neuropsychiatric risk. Mechanistically, these compounds promote glial activation, oxidative stress, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, and gut microbiota alterations that converge on hippocampal and limbic dysfunction. Rodent and invertebrate studies show sex-, dose-, and exposure-window-dependent effects on anxiety-, depression-, and cognition-like behaviors, with developmental exposure mirroring prenatal nicotine effects. Human data, although limited, are convergent: poisoning case series document acute neuropsychiatric symptoms; biomonitoring studies in China, Japan, and Sri Lanka associate urinary metabolites with depression, anxiety, and a recognizable "neo-nicotinic" symptom cluster; in Mexico, studies of agricultural populations link pesticide mixtures to psychological distress, although neonicotinoid biomarkers have not yet been measured in that setting; and pediatric cohorts in China and Ecuador link prenatal and childhood exposure to impaired neurodevelopment, emotional symptoms, and hyperactivity. Collectively, this evidence is consistent with neonicotinoids being an underrecognized environmental risk factor for neuropsychiatric disorders, although the human data remain too fragmented to support causal inference and underscores the need for dedicated cohorts, expanded biomonitoring, and mechanistic research to inform regulatory assessment.

title: On the Limits of Efficiency in AI-Based Air Quality Monitoring for Health Risk Assessment.
abstract: Air pollution remains a leading global health risk, with chronic low-level toxicity documented below current regulatory limits. This has prompted calls to tighten air quality standards, yet the monitoring systems underlying risk assessment were not designed to operate at such low concentrations. Drawing on epidemiological evidence from the ELAPSE project on long-term exposure to major air pollutants, we develop a quantitative model of how AI-based air quality monitoring (AQM) quality affects the hazard ratio from Cox proportional hazards models. We show that AQM error systematically attenuates the estimated hazard ratio toward the null, and that this attenuation intensifies as concentrations decline. The reliability of the risk estimate is bounded above by the validation accuracy of the AI exposure model. Because the deep learning component of AQM error has an irreducible floor, increasing model complexity cannot eliminate the attenuation. We derive a quantitative sufficiency criterion that identifies the AQM accuracy beyond which further improvement yields no toxicologically meaningful gain and accumulates technical debt. The analysis identifies the epidemiological design, not the monitoring system, as the binding constraint on the accuracy of toxicity assessment at low concentrations, and provides a quantitative basis for deciding whether further investment in AQM is justified.

title: Metal-Induced Neuro-Ototoxicity Evidence from Experimental Models.
abstract: Hearing loss is a major global health burden, and increasing evidence indicates that environmental and occupational exposure to neurotoxic metals may contribute to auditory dysfunction. This narrative review aimed to synthesize experimental evidence on metal-induced neuro-ototoxicity, with particular emphasis on morphological and functional alterations affecting peripheral and central components of the auditory system. A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar, focusing on animal studies investigating lead, mercury, cadmium, arsenic, and chromium exposure and auditory outcomes. Experimental evidence demonstrates that these metals can induce cochlear hair-cell injury, particularly involving outer hair cells and basal cochlear regions, as well as ribbon synapse loss, spiral ganglion dysfunction, and alterations of the stria vascularis. Central auditory effects include disrupted neural conduction, altered auditory brainstem responses, glial activation, synaptic dysfunction, and changes within the cochlear nucleus and inferior colliculus. Across metals, oxidative and nitrative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, calcium dysregulation, and regulated cell death emerge as interconnected mechanisms. Notably, auditory synaptopathy and central auditory dysfunction may occur with limited overt hair-cell loss. These findings support a multisite model of metal-induced neuro-ototoxicity and highlight the importance of evaluating both peripheral and central auditory pathways in experimental toxicology and environmental health research.

title: Lead (Pb)-Induced Neuroinflammation in the Developing and Aging Brain.
abstract: Dysregulation of neuroinflammation has been implicated as a key mechanism in the etiology of several conditions of both a developmental and degenerative nature. Neuroinflammation is also one of the main mechanisms by which contamination with certain environmental pollutants-like lead (Pb)-disrupts the central nervous system (CNS), leading to significant neurological damage. A growing body of evidence indicates a potential link between lead exposure to the onset of neurodevelopmental disorders-such as Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) and Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)-and neurodegenerative conditions, like those observed in Parkinson's disease (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD). Important pathways have been identified in the context of lead exposure and association with neurological conditions; however, the precise mechanisms by which lead-induced neuroinflammation might be associated with these conditions are largely unknown. Inflammation of the CNS can be considered a key element in the convergence of lead-induced neuroinflammation and neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative conditions. This review contextualizes aspects of neuroinflammatory responses upon lead exposure and discusses how these disruptions overlap with the onset of neurodevelopmental disorders, such as ASD and ADHD, and neurodegenerative diseases, such as PD and AD. We focus on recent developments in the field of neuroinflammation within these different contexts and discuss different hypotheses, sex as a biological variable, and areas in need of further investigation.

title: Investigating the Physiologic Effects of Repetitive Tibial Nerve Stimulation Treating Detrusor Overactivity in Rats.
journal: Neuromodulation : journal of the International Neuromodulation Society
abstract: Tibial nerve stimulation (TNS) effectively treats overactive bladder (OAB), but long-term application is frequently hindered by a progressive decline in therapeutic efficacy. This study aimed to investigate the mechanisms underlying this gradual attenuation associated with repetitive daily TNS (R-TNS) in OAB treatment. Using a cyclophosphamide-induced chronic detrusor overactivity (DO) rat model, we compared the urodynamic, electrophysiologic, and histomorphometric outcomes of acute TNS versus a seven-day continuous repetitive stimulation protocol. Urodynamically, although both modalities ameliorated DO symptoms, R-TNS yielded a lower intercontraction interval improvement (1.91 ± 0.38 minute) compared with acute stimulation (2.18 ± 0.39 minute), indicating therapeutic attenuation. Electrophysiologically, R-TNS significantly reduced both maximum amplitude and motor nerve conduction velocity (both p < 0.001). Crucially, hematoxylin and eosin staining confirmed the absence of axonal degeneration, Wallerian degeneration, or myofiber necrosis. However, Masson staining and Luxol fast blue staining revealed mild interstitial collagen deposition and scattered myelin loss, respectively, in the R-TNS group. This study systematically establishes a causal relationship between R-TNS efficacy attenuation and peripheral neural fatigue. The decline in sustained therapeutic efficacy is not caused by destructive pathology but rather by biophysical habituation characterized by myelin changes and mild fibrosis. Stimulation-induced fatigue acts as the primary barrier to R-TNS, underscoring the critical need to optimize clinical neuromodulation protocols.

title: A Multi-Omics and Systems Biology Perspective on the Potential Inverse Association Between Alzheimer's Disease and Glioblastoma: A Hypothesis-Generating Narrative Review.
abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and glioblastoma (GBM) are characterized by opposing cellular phenotypes (neurodegeneration versus uncontrolled proliferation) and have been considered for a long time as unrelated, but have been increasingly studied in the last decade because of their major individual, social, and economic burden. Several recent epidemiological studies reported an inverse association between AD and brain cancers, yet the biological basis of this relationship remains incompletely understood. Objective and Methods: This work aims to synthesise current evidence on the potential inverse relationship between AD and GBM, considering shared molecular pathways and divergent regulatory mechanisms through a multi-omics and systems-biology approach. Results: Multi-omics data reveal that AD and GBM share overlapping molecular pathways related to cell cycle regulation, apoptosis, metabolism, and immune responses, but exhibit opposite patterns of regulation. Transcriptomic analyses suggest inverse gene expression signatures, while proteomic and metabolomic studies highlight contrasting states of protein homeostasis and energy metabolism. Epigenetic modifications further contribute to disease-specific regulatory landscapes. Systems biology approaches identify key hub nodes, such as p53 and the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, that may act as molecular switches between neurodegeneration and tumorigenesis. Conclusions: The potential inverse association between AD and GBM observed in epidemiological studies may reflect differential modulation of shared biological networks, although GBM-specific evidence remains limited. This multi-omics perspective is consistent with a conceptual neurodegeneration-tumorigenesis axis, proposed here as an interpretive framework rather than an experimentally validated mechanism, and suggests candidate nodes warranting functional investigation.

title: A Two-Stage Questionnaire for Identifying Possible Parkinson's Disease: Machine-Learning Feature Selection and Interim Prospective Validation in Almaty, Kazakhstan.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a rapidly growing cause of neurological disability, yet diagnosis is often delayed in settings with limited access to movement-disorder specialists, including Kazakhstan and other Central Asian countries. This study aimed to develop a brief, self-administered, two-stage machine-learning-derived questionnaire based on binary symptom responses to identify individuals with possible clinically manifest PD who may benefit from specialist neurological assessment, and to evaluate its performance. Methods: From outpatient records of 402 patients with confirmed PD, a preliminary 100-item yes/no questionnaire was compiled. In a development cohort of 389 participants aged 60 to 90 years (146 with PD, 243 controls) recruited in Almaty, Kazakhstan, we used ElasticNet logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting to select features, reducing the instrument to 35 items (15 in Stage 1, 20 in Stage 2). We assessed performance on a held-out test set (n = 78) and in an interim prospective external-validation cohort (n = 290) recruited independently, with neurologists blinded to questionnaire results. Results: On the held-out test set, sensitivity was 86.2%, specificity 89.8%, accuracy 88.5%, and Stage 1 AUC 0.9557. In the interim external validation, sensitivity was 95.1%, specificity 94.4%, accuracy 94.5%, NPV 99.2%, and Stage 1 AUC 0.9962; only 12.1% of participants required Stage 2. Conclusions: The two-stage questionnaire showed strong case-finding ability in identifying individuals who warrant neurological evaluation. Findings are interim; completion of external validation, larger geographically diverse cohorts, and comparison against existing instruments are needed before wider implementation.

title: Neuroprotective Effects and Mechanisms of Cannabinoids in In Vitro Cell Models of Neurodegenerative Diseases: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease (HD), and Multiple sclerosis (MS) collectively affect millions of people worldwide, and substantial unmet needs remain for therapies that preserve neuronal structure and function. Current treatments can alleviate symptoms or modify selected disease processes, but they do not comprehensively target the interconnected cellular mechanisms that drive neuronal and axonal injury. Natural, semisynthetic, and synthetic cannabinoids have shown neuroprotective activity in preclinical models, but most remain at an early experimental stage, and their mechanisms of action have not been systematically mapped across disease contexts. Objective: This scoping review maps preclinical evidence, predominantly in vitro, with select studies incorporating in vivo validation, on exogenous cannabinoids and their neuroprotective mechanisms across cellular models of AD, PD, HD, and MS. The compounds examined include phytocannabinoids, synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists, and cannabinoid-active phytochemicals (e.g., β-amyrin, as described by the original study authors). Methods: This review followed JBI methodological guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting standards. The protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; 10.17605/OSF.IO/TAQ9F). PubMed, MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Web of Science were searched, yielding 8484 records (2844 after deduplication). Following two-stage screening in Rayyan, 194 reports were sought for full-text retrieval; 176 were assessed for eligibility, and 26 preclinical studies (2015-2025) met the inclusion criteria. Results: Most included studies were exclusively in vitro (n = 17); six combined in vitro and in vivo methods, and three combined in vitro methods with in silico or ex vivo components. The studies addressed AD (n = 11), PD (n = 8), general neuroinflammation models (n = 5), HD (n = 1), and MS (n = 1). Cannabidiol (CBD) was the most frequently studied compound (n = 9), followed by the synthetic agonists JWH-133 and ACEA (n = 6 combined), THC and its analogs (n = 5), and WIN 55,212-2 (n = 4). Evidence converged on three mechanistic domains: (1) anti-neuroinflammatory signaling in microglia and astrocytes; (2) antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial pathways; and (3) protein aggregate clearance, autophagy, myelination, and neurotransmitter modulation. Receptor pharmacology emerged as a cross-cutting axis linking these domains, rather than a fourth, parallel mechanism. It spanned canonical cannabinoid receptor type 1 and type 2 (CB1R/CB2R) signaling, non-canonical receptors (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ), G protein-coupled receptor 55 (GPR55), adenosine A2A receptor [A2AR], and transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1)), and receptor heteromerization. Conclusions: Cannabinoid-mediated neuroprotection in AD, PD, HD and MS cannot be explained by canonical receptor pharmacology alone. Three of 26 studies also reported receptor-independent or off-target mechanisms and formulation-dependent effects, highlighting potentially important but under-investigated contributors to cannabinoid-mediated neuroprotection. Translation priorities include systematic dose-response characterization, development of central nervous system (CNS)-penetrant CB2R agonists, and target-deconvolution studies to establish the prevalence of receptor-independent mechanisms and direct molecular effects.

title: Atypical Presentations in Patients with Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: A Retrospective Study of 106 Patients.
abstract: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is the most frequent entrapment neuropathy and is usually associated with classic sensory and motor findings. In rare cases, atypical presentations of CTS may occur, such as pruritus, Raynaud's phenomenon (RP), and digital ulceration. Our objective is to describe the clinical and electrodiagnostic (EDX) features of patients with CTS who exhibited these uncommon presentations. This is a review of patients referred for EDX confirmation of CTS, who also had unusual features such as pruritus, RP, and/or digital ulceration over a 12½ year period (1 January 2013-31 July 2026). All patients underwent detailed clinical examination and EDX studies. A total of 106 patients had evidence of CTS with uncommon features: pruritus in 92 (86.8%), RP in 8 (7.5%), digital ulceration in 4 (3.8%), and a combination of pruritus and RP in 1 (0.94%) and digital ulceration and RP in 1 (0.94%). Pruritus was associated with CTS in a total of 137 hands (48 patients unilateral and 45 patients bilateral). Of the 137 hands, the most common location of the pruritus was the palm in 72 (52.6%). A total of 132 (96.4%) of those patients had decreased pinprick sensation, and 21 (15.3%) had weakness and/or wasting of thenar muscles. CTS was graded as moderately severe in 67 (48.9%) of the 137 hands with pruritus. RP was associated with CTS in a total of 16 hands (4 patients unilateral and 6 patients bilateral). All 16 (100%) patients with RP had decreased pinprick sensation, and 3 (18.8%) patients had weakness and/or wasting of the thenar muscles. The CTS associated with RP was mild in 7 (43.8%) patients and moderate in 5 (31.2%). Ulcerative CTS was observed in a total of 7 hands (3 patients unilateral and 2 patients bilateral). All 7 patients with ulcerative CTS had either loss of sensation or hypoesthesia as well as weakness and/or wasting of the thenar muscles. The CTS was severe in all 7 of these patients. The severity of CTS varied by the type of CTS (pruritus, RP, and digital ulceration) (p-value < 0.001). Patients with digital ulceration had more severe symptoms than those with other presentations of CTS (p-value < 0.001). Patients with RP more frequently had mild symptoms compared to those with other presentations of CTS (p-value = 0.01). It is important for physicians of different specialties to be aware of rare, atypical clinical presentations of patients with CTS. These presentations include pruritus, RP limited to median nerve-innervated digits, and digital ulceration. These patients should be promptly referred for EDX studies to confirm the diagnosis of CTS.

title: Group Cohesion and Salivary Oxytocin During a Six-Month Coordination-Based Training Program in Junior Handball Players: A Prospective Non-Randomized Controlled Intervention Study.
abstract: Whether coordination-based training can develop group cohesion in youth sport, and how cohesion relates to peripheral oxytocin, is unclear. We examined cohesion and salivary oxytocin during a six-month coordination- and cohesion-oriented program in junior handball players. Sixty-four male players (12-14 years) from four clubs joined a prospective, non-randomized, within-club controlled study (not prospectively registered). In each club, one pre-existing training slot (eight players) formed the experimental group (EG; n = 32) and the other the control group (CG; n = 32). For 24 weeks (three sessions/week), EG replaced 20-25 min of technical-tactical work with coordination, cooperation, and interpersonal-synchrony exercises. The primary outcome was Youth Sport Environment Questionnaire (YSEQ) Task Cohesion. In the baseline-adjusted, cluster-robust analysis, T1 Task Cohesion was 0.72 points higher in EG than CG (95% CI 0.22-1.23; p = 0.010); Social Cohesion differed similarly (adjusted difference 0.77 points; 95% CI 0.33-1.22; p = 0.003). The adjusted oxytocin difference was imprecise and non-significant (5.0 pg/mL; 95% CI -0.01 to 10.02; p = 0.050), and oxytocin change was unrelated to Task Cohesion change. The program was accompanied by a more favorable cohesion trajectory than time-matched standard training. Non-randomized allocation precludes causal conclusions; oxytocin findings remain exploratory.

title: Urinary 3-Phenoxybenzoic Acid in U.S. Children and Adolescents: Temporal and Demographic Patterns in NHANES, 1999-2002 and 2007-2018.
abstract: Background: Pyrethroid pesticides are widely used, and children may experience exposure through multiple nonoccupational pathways. Urinary 3-phenoxybenzoic acid (3-PBA) is a commonly used biomarker of recent pyrethroid exposure. Methods: In this repeated cross-sectional analysis, we analyzed U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data for participants aged 3-19 years from 1999-2002 and 2007-2018. Urinary 3-PBA data were unavailable for 2003-2006. Descriptive statistics for urinary 3-PBA concentrations were creatinine-corrected and estimated by age group and survey cycle. For regression analyses, urinary 3-PBA concentrations were not creatinine-corrected; instead, log-transformed urinary 3-PBA was modeled with urinary creatinine included as a covariate, along with survey cycle, age group, sex, race/ethnicity, and poverty-income ratio (PIR). Analyses incorporated subsample weights with SUDAAN software. Results: Among 7415 U.S. children and adolescents, the overall creatinine-corrected geometric mean urinary 3-PBA concentrations were 0.31 [95% CI: 0.25, 0.39] and 0.93 [0.80, 1.08] µg/g creatinine for survey cycles 1999-2000 and 2017-2018, respectively. Concentrations were higher in younger children than in older children. Urinary 3-PBA concentrations were generally higher in later survey cycles. Adjusted models showed that urinary 3-PBA concentrations were higher among younger children and children from lower-income households and were lower among non-Hispanic Black, Mexican American, and Other race/ethnicity groups compared with non-Hispanic White children. Survey cycle was positively associated with urinary 3-PBA in the 1999-2002 and 2007-2014 model but was not statistically significant in the 2015-2018 model. Sex was not consistently associated with urinary 3-PBA across the two analytic periods. Conclusions: Recent pyrethroid exposure, as reflected by urinary 3-PBA, was widespread and socially patterned among U.S. children and adolescents. Urinary 3-PBA varied by age group, survey cycle, race/ethnicity, and poverty-income ratio. These findings should be interpreted as exposure surveillance data rather than evidence of specific health effects. Ongoing biomonitoring, source-focused research, and studies with repeated exposure assessments would help to better understand the factors influencing pyrethroid exposure and its public health significance in children.

title: Associations Between Long-Term High-Altitude Exposure and Cognitive Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Studies on Event-Related Potentials.
abstract: Although long-term high-altitude (HA) exposure is associated with cognitive alterations, evidence regarding the corresponding event-related potential (ERP) components is inconsistent, and a systematic synthesis across processing stages is lacking. This meta-analysis synthesized available ERP evidence to examine neurophysiological alterations associated with cognitive processing following long-term HA exposure. The most consistent finding was a reduction in P300 amplitude among the HA groups (g = -0.476). Reduced P100 amplitude was also observed (g = -0.325), although this finding was less robust, with a possible small-study-effect signal. Rotation-related negativity amplitude was more negative in HA groups (g = -0.748), but this estimate was based on only four independent studies. No reliable between-group differences were observed for other evaluated ERP outcomes. Moderator analyses provided limited evidence of systematic moderation and are constrained by low statistical power. Overall, the available evidence is heterogeneous and primarily based on cross-sectional comparisons. These findings suggest possible stage-dependent associations between long-term HA exposure and ERP alterations, although rigorous longitudinal studies using standardized ERP protocols are needed to substantiate these associations.

title: Synaptobrevin JMD-TMD Regions Induce Robust Lipid Disorder, Membrane Remodeling and PIP2-Dependent Cluster Formation.
abstract: Synaptobrevin (Syb/VAMP) is the vesicular SNARE that drives synaptic vesicle fusion. Before fusion, Syb is located in the vesicle membrane. After fusion, Syb is translocated to the presynaptic plasma membrane and exposed to a different lipid environment. How its membrane-proximal juxtamembrane and transmembrane domains (JMD-TMDs) organize these different surrounding membrane environments remains incompletely understood. Here, we used MARTINI coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations in planar membrane models to investigate Syb1/2 membrane organization and collective behavior. Syb1 and Syb2 induced similar and robust local lipid disorder, whereas the spatial organization of lipid disorder and membrane mismatch depended more strongly on membrane lipid composition. In ten-copy systems, mean cluster sizes over the final 100 ns were approximately 30% lower for wild-type Syb1 and 39% lower for wild-type Syb2 in PIP2-depleted than in the corresponding PIP2-containing plasma membranes. Collective Syb assembly was accompanied by pronounced PIP2 redistribution and strong local enrichment, whereas PS showed substantially weaker local enrichment when both lipid species were present. Clustering spatially overlapped otherwise localized lipid-disordered regions without proportionally amplifying their magnitude. The applicability of these findings to curved vesicles and fusion or endocytic intermediates remains to be established. Together, these results distinguish robust local membrane disorder from composition-dependent geometric remodeling and identify PIP2 as a prominent correlate of higher-order Syb organization that may contribute to post-fusion Syb reorganization before endocytic retrieval.

title: Modulation of the Activity of Voltage-Gated Potassium Channels Kv1.3 by the Flavonols Quercetin and Morin.
abstract: The aim of this study was to determine whether quercetin-mediated Kv1.3 inhibition is a general flavonol effect or compound-specific. The impact of quercetin and morin-differing by a single B-ring hydroxyl-on the endogenous Kv1.3 current in Jurkat T was compared. Currents were recorded using whole-cell patch-clamp across the 30-105 µM concentration range. Quercetin inhibited the current abruptly: no effect at 30 µM, a 40% reduction at 60 µM, followed 50% reduction in higher concentrations. Morin inhibited the current throughout the range, but its effect depended marginally on concentration. No changes in activation or inactivation kinetics were detected, and inhibition reversed upon washout. The 48 h MTT-assessed viability IC50 for quercetin was 6.25 µM, an order of magnitude below current-inhibiting concentrations, and 30.1 µM for morin. Additionally, quercetin at 30 µM, inactive alone, combined with simvastatin (6 µM), left only a quarter of the current-well below the predicted value, though exploratory testing did not establish synergy. This study reports morin's action on Kv1.3 in Jurkat cells for the first time, showing that both flavonols inhibit the channel but that the attainable extent of inhibition is compound-specific.

title: MAMs and Diabetic Cardiomyopathy: Research Progress on Calcium Homeostasis Regulatory Mechanisms.
abstract: Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a highly specific cardiovascular complication of diabetes that occurs independently of hypertension and coronary atherosclerotic heart disease, and is primarily characterized by diffuse myocardial fibrosis and impaired diastolic and systolic function. In recent years, mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs), as dynamic membrane contact points connecting the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, have attracted much attention in maintaining calcium homeostasis in myocardial cells, regulating energy metabolism and cell survival fate. This article systematically reviews the structural composition of MAMs and their core roles in apoptosis, mitophagy, inflammatory response and calcium homeostasis regulation. It focuses on the molecular mechanisms by which FUNDC1/IP3R2, Bmal1/Bcl-2/IP3R and PPARα/Mfn2 MAM-related signaling pathways mediate calcium overload in DCM, and reviews the research progress of drugs such as dapagliflozin, ferulic acid, quercetin, and ginsenoside Rb1 in improving DCM by targeting the MAM-calcium homeostasis axis. Finally, this review discusses the key scientific issues and future translational research directions in this field, aiming to provide references for mechanism research and new drug development in DCM.

title: From Coastal Residue to Bioactive Resource: Antioxidant and Anti-Inflammatory Potential of Beach-Cast Posidonia oceanica.
abstract: Beach-cast Posidonia oceanica represents an abundant Mediterranean marine biomass that is commonly perceived as coastal waste, despite its potential value within circular bioeconomy strategies. This study investigated the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory potential of a hydroethanolic extract obtained from beach-cast P. oceanica biomass (POE). The extract was chemically profiled by UHPLC-ESI-MS/MS and evaluated through spectrophotometric antioxidant assays, including total phenolic content, total flavonoid content, reducing power, ABTS and DPPH radical-scavenging assays. Its ability to protect plasmid DNA from oxidative damage was also assessed. Anti-inflammatory activity was investigated in LPS-stimulated RAW 264.7 macrophages by evaluating cell viability, intracellular ROS production, NO release, iNOS and COX-2 expression, NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation and MAPK phosphorylation. POE showed measurable phenolic and flavonoid contents, moderate antioxidant capacity and protection against H2O2/Fe2+-induced plasmid DNA damage. UHPLC-ESI-MS/MS analysis revealed a complex metabolite profile, with 156 annotated compounds distributed across 20 chemical classes. In macrophages, POE was not cytotoxic at 50 and 100 µg/mL and significantly reduced LPS-induced ROS and NO production. These effects were accompanied by decreased iNOS and COX-2 expression, inhibition of NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation and reduced phosphorylation of p38, ERK and JNK. In addition, POE showed no detectable cytotoxicity in NIH3T3 fibroblasts up to 10 mg/mL and no mutagenic activity in the Ames MPF™ assay using TA98 and TA100 strains, either in the absence or presence of metabolic activation. Overall, this exploratory study suggests that beach-cast P. oceanica retains bioactive properties, although further studies incorporating standardized collection protocols and quantitative chemical characterization will help clarify its potential for sustainable valorisation.

title: The Cardiopulmonary-Brain Axis Hypothesis in Fontan Physiology.
journal: Journal of cardiovascular development and disease
abstract: Advances in surgical and medical management have improved survival for individuals with Fontan physiology (FP), increasing attention to long-term neurocognitive impairments. We propose the Cardiopulmonary-Brain Axis Hypothesis, identifying respiratory muscle performance (RMP) as a potentially modifiable contributor to executive function in FP. Drawing on evidence from cardiovascular and respiratory physiology, autonomic neuroscience, cerebrovascular biology, and neurocognitive research, this framework explores potential relationships among RMP, FP, respiratory muscle metaboreflex activation, autonomic regulation, cerebral perfusion, and executive function. Fontan-specific studies demonstrate the influence of respiration on venous return and pulmonary blood flow, while selected inspiratory muscle training (IMT) studies report improvements in respiratory function. Building on these findings, we hypothesize that improvements in RMP following IMT may enhance respiratory pump efficiency, favorably influence Fontan hemodynamics, attenuate respiratory muscle metaboreflex activation, and support autonomic regulation and cerebral perfusion, with potential downstream improvements in executive function. However, evidence supporting these relationships varies, with several mechanisms derived primarily from non-Fontan populations. The pathway remains untested, and improvements in executive function following IMT have not been established in FP. The Cardiopulmonary-Brain Axis Hypothesis provides a biologically plausible, testable framework to guide future longitudinal and interventional investigations examining the potential relationships between RMP, cardiopulmonary function, and brain health.

title: Hemoglobin-to-RDW Ratio and All-Cause Mortality in Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis: Complementary Value to Echocardiographic Right Ventricular-Pulmonary Arterial Coupling.
journal: Journal of cardiovascular development and disease
abstract: Background: The hemoglobin-to-red cell distribution width ratio (HRR) is a composite hematologic biomarker that integrates oxygen-carrying capacity and inflammation-related erythrocyte variability. Its prognostic value in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), and its relationship with right ventricular (RV) function, have not been established. Methods: We conducted a single-center retrospective study of 198 patients with IPF. A total of 165 patients with baseline hemoglobin, red cell distribution width (RDW) and date of diagnosis available constituted the analytical cohort. An HRR cutoff (≤0.86) was derived by time-dependent Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis at 5 years. All-cause mortality from diagnosis was assessed by Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression, with bootstrap internal validation. Associations between hematologic markers and TAPSE (Tricuspid Annular Plane Systolic Excursion), PAPs (pulmonary arterial systolic pressure) and TAPSE/PASP were examined by linear and logistic regression, followed by joint stratification of HRR and RV-PA coupling. Results: Over a median follow-up of 70.3 months, 57 patients (34.5%) died. Low HRR was associated with higher mortality (72.7% vs. 15.5%; adjusted HR 3.07, 95% CI 1.68-5.63; optimism-corrected HR 2.37) and improved a clinical model beyond RDW (likelihood-ratio p = 0.012). HRR was not associated with TAPSE, PAPs, TAPSE/PASP or RV-PA uncoupling. In exploratory joint stratification, mortality rose from 11.7% with both markers preserved to 100% with both abnormal (age-adjusted HR 6.47, 95% CI 2.64-15.86). At 5 years, HRR and RDW showed similar discrimination (time-dependent AUC 0.70 and 0.71), higher than TAPSE/PASP (0.61). Conclusions: HRR is a simple, inexpensive and independent predictor of mortality in IPF that is unrelated to RV-PA coupling. The two markers provide complementary prognostic information, and their combination identifies a subgroup at very high risk. These findings require external validation.

title: Influence of Implant Macrodesign on Primary Stability Across Different Bone Density Models: A Comparative In Vitro Study.
abstract: Implant macrogeometry and bone density are major determinants of primary stability. This study aimed to evaluate primary stability across different implant macrodesigns and block models. A total of 153 implants were divided into Group 1 (AnyRidge), Group 2 (BlueDiamond RC), and Group 3 (BlueDiamond NC) (n = 51 each). Each implant was sequentially tested in synthetic D1-D4 bone models. Insertion torque values (ITV) and implant stability quotient (ISQ) were recorded. In D1, ITV was highest in Group 1 (69.51 ± 1.50 Ncm), followed by Group 2 (53.82 ± 6.75 Ncm) and Group 3 (49.31 ± 7.00 Ncm) (p < 0.01, p < 0.001). In D4, ITV decreased to 34.71 ± 3.23, 19.90 ± 3.08, and 11.18 ± 2.14 Ncm, respectively (p < 0.001). D1 ISQ values were 84.53 ± 2.51, 72.08 ± 3.69, and 66.33 ± 2.63, respectively (p < 0.001). In D4, ISQ values were 60.29 ± 3.84, 52.86 ± 3.73, and 52.18 ± 2.48, respectively (p < 0.001); Groups 2 and 3 did not differ significantly. Implant macrodesign influences primary stability, with AnyRidge demonstrating the highest ITV and ISQ values in D1 as well as D4. Further clinical studies would be beneficial to support these findings.

title: Does Tumor-Mask Guidance Improve Glioma Grade Classification from T2-Weighted MRI Alone? An Out-of-Fold Evaluation with nnU-Net and Ground-Truth Localization.
abstract: Multi-sequence MRI is the standard for glioma assessment, but complete or contrast-enhanced protocols are not always available (withheld gadolinium, low-field MRI, incomplete archives). We asked whether tumor localization improves grade classification from T2-weighted MRI alone. In this retrospective study of the BraTS2020 training cohort (369 patients; legacy labels 293 high-grade [HGG], 76 low-grade [LGG]), 74 patients (15 LGG) were held out at the patient level for internal testing. A 2D U-Net trained in five development folds supplied out-of-fold whole-tumor masks for training 3D CNN classifiers; nnU-Net served as a segmentation benchmark. Classifiers received T2 alone or T2 plus a mask, which at test time came from the 2D U-Net, nnU-Net, the ground truth (oracle) or random noise. Analyses used five seeds, DeLong tests with Holm correction and development-set cross-validation. Whole-tumor Dice was 0.807 (95% CI 0.773-0.840) for the 2D U-Net and 0.877 (0.857-0.895) for nnU-Net. The T2-only CNN reached an ROC-AUC of 0.814 (95% CI 0.702-0.913). Mask-guided variants reached 0.677-0.742, none above T2-only (Holm-adjusted p = 1.00 for all four confirmatory comparisons of informative masks). Cross-validation reproduced this ranking (0.782 vs. 0.707). With LGG as the positive class, PR-AUC was 0.571 (no-skill 0.203). Tumor-mask guidance did not improve T2-only grading at any level of mask quality, including ground truth. The results concern a legacy grade label in one public cohort and require external testing.

title: Peri-Implant Femoral Fractures Around Intramedullary Nails: A Multicenter Case Series.
abstract: Background: Peri-implant fractures following intramedullary nailing of femoral fractures are an increasing concern in elderly orthopedic trauma patients. These fractures pose significant clinical challenges due to altered load transmission in osteoporotic bone, comorbidities and complex fracture patterns. Optimal management remains unclear and secondary prevention strategies such as osteoporosis treatment are underutilized. Materials and Methods: This retrospective multicenter study analyzed 11 patients who sustained peri-implant fractures after intramedullary femoral nailing between 2015 and 2022. Data collected included demographics, comorbidities, fracture characteristics, implant details, postoperative rehabilitation protocols, complications and functional outcomes measured by WOMAC and SF-12 scores. Results: The mean patient age was 85 years, with fractures most frequently occurring at the distal and proximal nail tips. Cardiovascular comorbidities were prevalent, with an mean Charlson Comorbidity Index of 4.27. Nearly half the fractures followed low-energy trauma such as falls. Complications affected 45.5% of patients and included infections, myocardial infarction, periprosthetic fracture and one death. Among available postoperative assessments, the mean WOMAC score was 49.0 (n = 10), and the mean SF-12 physical component score was 25.0 (n = 11). Functional outcomes were generally poor and only one patient was on anti-osteoporotic therapy. The small cohort does not allow reliable identification of implant-related risk factors. Conclusions: A personalized treatment framework integrating fracture morphology, implant stability, bone stock, comorbidity burden, joint status, and rehabilitation potential is clinically relevant, although this descriptive series cannot validate a decision algorithm. Peri-implant fractures in elderly, comorbid patients represent a complex clinical problem with high complication rates and poor functional recovery. The low rate of osteoporosis treatment highlights an important area for improvement. Management should be tailored to fracture morphology, existing fixation, bone stock, associated joint disease, and patient frailty. Larger prospective studies are needed to establish standardized treatment protocols and improve patient outcomes.

title: Interpreting Abnormal Neural Activity in Neurological Disorders Through Human iPSC Models.
abstract: Abnormal neural activity is observed across neurological disorders, yet similar firing and network phenotypes can arise from distinct physiological disturbances. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models have advanced research from describing disease-associated activity changes to identifying the cellular processes that generate and modify them. This review integrates cross-disease comparisons, physiological measurements, and targeted interventions to distinguish the cellular mechanisms underlying similar neural activity phenotypes. TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) dependent KCNQ2 splice correction restores potassium conductance and firing regulation, whereas 3,5-dihydroxyphenylglycine (DHPG) treatment improves network burst organization and reduces hypersynchrony in SHANK2 mutant cultures. This comparison identifies distinct forms of functional recovery that cannot be inferred from activity direction alone. Across neurological disorders, neuronal development, cellular composition, and interactions with neighboring cells further influence the expression of abnormal activity. Comparing physiological endpoints with intervention controls clarifies which neuronal functions are recovered and the extent to which their recovery supports specific mechanistic conclusions.

title: The Developing Injured Brain Is Not Quiet: Rapid Region Specific Axonal Injury and Microglia Activation Within the First Day Following a Diffuse Traumatic Brain Injury in a Pediatric Rat Model.
abstract: Pediatric traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of death and disability in children. Despite pediatric TBI's prevalence, its underlying progression of cellular outcomes are largely extrapolated from adult studies. Notably, axonal injury and acute microglial activation following pediatric TBI remains under-characterized. We addressed this gap by utilizing a central fluid percussion injury (cFPI) model in postnatal day 16-18 male and female rats to investigate axonal injury burden, microglia morphological and Iba-1 fluorescence intensity changes acutely following sham or cFPI in the lateral cortex (CTX), subcortical white matter (SCWM) and thalamus (THAL). Microscopic assessment revealed diffuse axonal injury within the CTX, SCWM, and THAL with different temporal progressions that largely resolved within 1 d post-injury. Microglial morphology changed significantly 1 h post-injury in the CTX and THAL and 3 h post-cFPI in the SCWM. Interestingly, microglial morphological changes were observed to precede axonal-injury-associated APP accumulation, indicating a temporal difference between the two markers. These findings demonstrate rapid, region-specific, and temporally distinct microglia morphological changes and responses following diffuse TBI. Additionally, utilizing high-dimensional morphological profiling can define microglia responses in the developing brain, potentially revealing novel therapeutic windows for pediatric TBI intervention.

title: Beyond Testosterone-The Androgen Receptor Exon-1 CAG Repeat from Molecular Mechanism and Kennedy Disease to Compensated Androgen Resistance and a Research Framework for Precision Endocrinology.
abstract: The biological effect of testosterone cannot be inferred from its circulating concentration alone. Androgen action is determined jointly by ligand availability, tissue steroid metabolism, androgen-receptor (AR) abundance and function, coregulatory context, and hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular feedback. A polymorphic CAG repeat in exon 1 of the X-linked AR gene encodes a variable polyglutamine tract in the intrinsically disordered N-terminal transactivation domain. Pathogenic expansion causes spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA; Kennedy disease), in which partial androgen insensitivity coexists with an androgen-dependent toxic gain of function. Within the non-SBMA range, longer repeats usually-but not invariably-reduce AR-mediated transcription in experimental systems and may shift the relationship between serum testosterone and androgen-responsive phenotypes. This critical translational review integrates the molecular biochemistry, historical discovery, population diversity, endocrine compensation, organ-specific phenotypes, and pharmacogenetics of the AR CAG repeat. The evidence supports a graded, tissue-dependent effect rather than a universal molecular switch. SBMA provides compelling proof that long polyglutamine tracts impair aspects of canonical AR action, but its neurodegeneration reflects additional ligand-dependent proteotoxic mechanisms and cannot be extrapolated linearly to ordinary alleles. In population cohorts, longer common-range repeats are often accompanied by modestly higher total and free testosterone and sometimes higher estradiol, consistent with a shifted feedback set point. High luteinizing hormone is not obligatory. Phenotypic associations involving fertility, sexuality, body composition, metabolism, bone, mood, prostate, and cardiovascular traits are heterogeneous, whereas differential prostate and erythropoietic responses during testosterone therapy provide comparatively coherent pharmacogenetic signals. AR CAG length should therefore be considered a quantitative modifier of androgen action. A continuous CAG-by-testosterone response surface spanning 15-35 repeats is proposed as a transparent framework.

title: Oncohematology in the Era of Immunotherapies: The Key Role of the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) Complex.
abstract: Immunotherapy has transformed the therapeutic landscape of onco-hematology, evolving from historical allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) to modern chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T/NK cell therapies, bispecific antibodies, and immune checkpoint inhibitors. Central to this immunological cross-talk is the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) system, which governs self/non-self-discrimination, alloreactivity, and tumor immune evasion across both classical allografts and novel adoptive cellular platforms. Facing hematological malignancies, ranging from acute leukemias and multiple myeloma to chronic leukemias and lymphomas, clinicians must overcome tumor immune escape while managing treatment-related toxicities and Graft-versus-Host Disease (GvHD). Advances in high-throughput molecular biology techniques, notably Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) and long-read sequencing, have become indispensable for high-resolution HLA matching, minimal residual disease (MRD) monitoring, and chimerism analysis. Furthermore, gene-editing strategies (e.g., CRISPR/Cas9) targeting TRAC, B2M, and CIITA, alongside HLA-E engineering and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) technology, are driving the development of universal "off-the-shelf" effector platforms that bypass classic HLA barriers. In this review, we provide a conceptual synthesis of immunotherapeutic paradigms in onco-hematology, highlighting the pivotal role of HLA biology and molecular diagnostics in shaping next-generation personalized cellular therapies.

title: Cross-Disease Transcriptomic Analysis Identifies Selective Lysosomal Gene-Expression Patterns in Alzheimer's Disease and Lung Cancer.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and lung cancer show an inverse transcriptomic relationship, but how this genome-wide pattern is organized within the lysosomal system remains unclear. To address this question, a staged analysis combined the Sánchez-Valle primary bulk dataset, a Forés-Martos cross-study reproducibility assessment, a harmonized 73-gene lysosomal panel organized into seven functional modules, AD single-nucleus data, and matched lung cancer and AD myeloid resources. In Sánchez-Valle, 2965 of 4601 shared AD-lung cancer genes were reciprocal (64.4%), compared with 361 of 2171 shared AD-glioblastoma genes (16.6%). Forés-Martos reproduced reciprocal predominance, with 1187 of 1992 shared AD-lung cancer genes reciprocal (59.6%). Within the lysosomal panel, reciprocal and concordant changes were intermingled across lysosomal functions. Thirteen of 28 jointly significant genes were reciprocal in Sánchez-Valle (46.4%) and 7 of 11 in Forés-Martos (63.6%), but neither the panel nor individual modules showed reciprocal enrichment beyond genome-wide backgrounds. CTSA, NEU1, ATP6V0E2, and ATP6V1C1 were reproducibly downregulated in AD and upregulated in lung cancer, whereas CTSH showed the opposite pattern; ATP6V1B2, ATP6V1E1, FIG4, and RRAGA were concordantly downregulated. In AD brain, lysosomal differential-expression burden was highest in oligodendrocytes (52.0%) and astrocytes (45.3%), with additional cell-type-specific patterns in microglia and neurons. In matched myeloid populations, 23 of 73 lysosomal genes were directionally matched, including 8 reciprocal and 15 same-direction genes, representing strong enrichment relative to the non-panel background (OR = 7.58, p = 1.11 × 10-11), while reciprocity was not preferentially enriched among directionally matched genes (34.8% vs. 48.6%, p = 0.211). Together, these findings define a heterogeneous lysosomal gene-expression pattern in which broad AD-lung cancer transcriptomic opposition is partitioned across functional programs and cell types, with no evidence for uniform pathway reversal.

title: Extracellular Vesicles in Ocular Immunoregulation: Context-Dependent Mechanisms and Translational Evidence.
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry immune signals between ocular cells. Their effects depend on the cell that releases them, its activation state, the recipient tissue, and the route of exposure. This narrative review examines endogenous EV signaling and administered EV preparations across the ocular surface, cornea, uvea, retina, and optic nerve. Donor corneal EVs can transfer alloantigens, and EVs from activated retinal glia can injure vascular cells. In experimental disease, selected stromal- and regulatory B-cell EVs reduce inflammation by altering antigen presentation, T-cell responses, or macrophage and microglial activity. Cargo perturbation supports some of these mechanisms, whereas many patient biofluid signatures remain associative. Two small dry-eye studies reported short-term improvements after topical treatment. Whether these benefits persist, or extend to other ocular diseases, remains unknown. Translation requires reproducible EV preparations, assays that predict activity in the target tissue, and controlled trials with longer follow-up.

title: Severe High-Thoracic Contusion Spinal Cord Injury Disrupts Acute Autonomic Function in Female Rats: Cardiovascular, Core Body Temperature, and Activity Implications.
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) disrupts supraspinal regulation of autonomic function, leading to altered cardiovascular, physiological, and behavioral outcomes that may contribute to long-term morbidity. However, acute autonomic alterations following severe high-thoracic (T3) contusion SCI remain poorly characterized. This study investigated continuous changes in activity, cardiovascular parameters, and core body temperature during the first week after contusion SCI. Telemetric implants were placed in the descending aorta of adult female Wistar rats to facilitate recording of activity, systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), heart rate (HR), and core body temperature. Two weeks after telemetry surgery and following 48 h of baseline recordings, rats received a T3 contusion SCI (400 kdyn, 5 s dwell time), followed by continuous telemetric monitoring from 1 to 7 days post-injury. SCI markedly reduced activity and significantly increased SBP, DBP, and MAP from 1 to 4 days post-injury. SCI also induced sustained tachycardia, altered heart rate variability (HRV), and caused hypothermia. In addition, SCI disrupted 24 h rhythms and day-night differences for several parameters. These findings provide a comprehensive assessment of acute autonomic dysfunction following severe high-thoracic contusion SCI and direct future research on experimental therapeutic interventions.

title: Functional CB1 and CB2 Receptors at Pallido-Nigral GABAergic Terminals-Activation by Endocannabinoids.
abstract: CB1 and CB2 receptors form a heteromer expressed in primate pallidal neurons. However, the presence and function of the receptors in rat globus pallidus neurons and their terminals remain unknown. We investigate the presence of CB1 and CB2 receptors on parvalbumin-positive neurons and their function in pallido-nigral terminals, and whether endocannabinoids can activate them. We detected mRNA for CB1 and CB2 receptors in pallidal neurons, and proteins co-expressed in PVA+ neurons. By PLA assay we found proximity of CB1 and CB2 proteins in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra reticulata. Both receptors co-precipitate in the nigral synaptosomes, whereas a pallidal kainic acid lesion decreases coprecipitation. Electrophysiological recordings of pallidal-nigral evoked IPSC GABAergic currents show that selective CB1r activation decreases GABA release, as indicated by a decrement in IPSC amplitude and a change in the paired-pulse ratio. In contrast, activation of CB2r did not modify release. Moreover, CB2r activation decreases the inhibition produced by CB1r. Depolarization suppression of inhibition (DSI) experiments confirmed the activation of CB1 and CB2Rs by endogenous endocannabinoids and the interaction whereby CB2r modulates the effect of CB1r inhibition. These data indicate interacting presynaptic CB1/CB2 receptors at pallido-nigral terminals, which are activated by endocannabinoids and control GABA release, probably reflecting the proposed heteromeric interaction.

title: Chronic Pain-Induced Adaptations in Mesolimbic Circuitry.
abstract: Chronic pain is frequently accompanied by emotional-affective symptoms that significantly contribute to patient morbidity and complicate pain management. Despite this, mechanisms underlying these symptoms are poorly understood, preventing the development of targeted therapies. Affective symptoms have been attributed to the development of a pain-related hypodopaminergic state through decreased activity of ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopamine neurons. However, accumulating evidence suggests that pain-related changes in VTA dopamine neuron activity are heterogeneous due to the cellular and functional diversity of the VTA and its projection targets. Here, we review clinical and preclinical evidence for pain-related VTA dysfunction with a focus on heterogeneity present in cellular and circuit mechanisms and their behavioral consequences. By integrating the sources of heterogeneity present in these studies, we suggest that pain-related affective dysfunction is best understood in the context of neurochemical identity, projection target, time, sex, pain etiology, and behavioral readout, challenging the framework of a generalized pain-related hypodopaminergic state.

title: Vitamin D and Vitamin K in Neuro-Oncology and Brain Metabolism: Emerging Roles in Gliomas, Neurodegeneration, and Metabolic Dysregulation.
abstract: Recent advances in micronutrient biology have highlighted the pleiotropic roles of vitamins D and K in central nervous system (CNS) health and disease. Beyond their classical functions in calcium homeostasis, both vitamins exhibit regulatory effects on inflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, and gene expression, positioning them as potential modulators in neuro-oncology and neurodegeneration.
