In gliomas, vitamin D has been shown to influence tumour cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis through vitamin D receptor (VDR)-mediated signalling, while vitamin K-particularly menaquinone-may influence glioma biology through vitamin K-dependent proteins, sphingolipid metabolism, and ferroptosis-related pathways. In neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, deficiencies in vitamins D and K have been associated with increased neuroinflammation, impaired neuronal survival, and dysregulated protein aggregation. Emerging evidence also suggests that these vitamins play a role in brain metabolic homeostasis, particularly in glucose utilization, insulin signalling, and lipid metabolism. This is especially relevant in conditions such as brain insulin resistance and neurodegeneration linked to metabolic syndrome, where disturbances in mitochondrial function and energy metabolism may also contribute to disease progression. This review synthesizes current findings on the shared and independent roles of vitamins D and K in glioma biology, neurodegenerative processes, and brain-related metabolic disorders. It further explores their therapeutic potential as adjunctive strategies in precision medicine, while identifying key gaps for future translational research. However, current evidence remains insufficient to establish either vitamin as a disease-modifying therapy.

title: DNA Methyltransferase Inhibitor Suppresses Corneal Scarring.
abstract: Corneal fibrosis and opacity are major causes of visual impairment and blindness, while the conventional treatment by corneal transplantation remains limited due to the global shortage of donor materials and the risk of immune-mediated graft rejection. In this study, we investigated DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) inhibition using the FDA-approved agent decitabine (DAC; 5-aza-2'-deoxycytidine) to suppress corneal fibrosis. DNMT3A is a predicted target of the anti-fibrotic microRNA miR-29a, which was previously linked to the scar-reducing effects of cornealstromal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (doi:10.1016/j.jare.2022.05.008). DNMT3A expression was upregulated in scarred mouse corneas. In donor-derived corneal stromal fibroblasts, DAC dose-dependently suppressed TGFβ1-induced αSMA expression and attenuated myofibroblast-associated morphological and functional changes, including collagen gel contraction, at concentrations up to 50 μM. RNA sequencing further showed that DAC reversed TGFβ1-driven extracellular matrix remodeling, including changes in SPOCK1 and CTHRC1 expression. These effects were supported in injured mouse corneas, where topical DAC treatment reduced SPOCK1 and CTHRC1 expression, decreased scar formation, and restored corneal thickness toward normal levels. Fibrosis- and inflammation-associated gene expression was also downregulated, with no apparent treatment-related toxicity. In conclusion, these findings demonstrate that DNMT inhibition suppresses corneal fibrosis and myofibroblast differentiation, supporting the repurposing of DAC as a pharmacological, donor-independent strategy for reducing corneal fibrosis and preserving corneal transparency.

title: Cytotoxic, Immunogenic Cell Death-Associated and Immunomodulatory Effects of Ruthenium(II) Terpyridine Complexes in Mesenchymal Stem Cells and CT26 Tumor-Bearing Mice.
abstract: Ruthenium-based complexes have emerged as promising alternatives to platinum-containing anticancer drugs because of their favorable pharmacological properties and potential immunomodulatory activity. However, their effects on mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), an important component of the tumor microenvironment, remain poorly understood. The biological effects of two ruthenium(II) terpyridine complexes (Ru-1 and Ru-2), compared with oxaliplatin as a reference compound, were investigated in mouse mesenchymal stem cells (mMSCs) using MTT, LDH, Annexin V/PI, cell-cycle and calreticulin exposure assays. Extracellular ATP and HMGB1 release were additionally assessed as immunogenic cell death-associated markers. The immunomodulatory effects of Ru-1 and Ru-2 were evaluated in healthy and CT26 tumor-bearing mice by flow cytometric analysis of lymphoid and myeloid-cell populations. Both ruthenium complexes induced concentration-dependent cytotoxicity in mMSCs, with Ru-1 consistently exhibiting greater cytotoxic activity than Ru-2 and potency comparable to that of oxaliplatin after 24 h of exposure. Notably, both complexes were more cytotoxic toward mMSCs than toward CT26 cells, indicating limited selectivity for malignant over bone marrow-derived stromal cells in vitro. In mMSC, cell death occurred predominantly through apoptosis and was accompanied by G2/M cell-cycle arrest. Both complexes also induced the emission of ICD-associated DAMPs, including calreticulin exposure and extracellular ATP and HMGB1 release, in mMSCs and CT26 cells. In vivo, Ru-1 increased the proportions of CD8+ T lymphocytes, NK cells and NKT cells in CT26 tumor-bearing mice, whereas in healthy mice, it increased NK and NKT cells without affecting T lymphocytes. Selected myeloid-cell and monocyte populations were also modulated, predominantly in healthy animals. This is the first study to characterize the biological effects of ruthenium(II) terpyridine complexes in mesenchymal stem cells alongside their in vivo immunomodulatory activity. Ru-1 elicits the emission of multiple damage-associated molecular patterns linked to immunogenic cell death in both tumor and stromal cell populations, although the functional immunogenicity of the induced cell death remains to be confirmed. These findings support further preclinical investigation of ruthenium(II) terpyridine complexes as potential immunomodulatory anticancer agents.

title: Tumor-Driven Innervation: Neoneurogenesis, Neural Mimicry, and Neuro-Immune Crosstalk in the Tumor Microenvironment.
abstract: Cancer is increasingly understood as a tissue- and system-level disease shaped by dynamic interactions among malignant cells, stromal elements, the vasculature, the immune system, and the nervous system. In this context, tumors are not passive recipients of neural input, but active participants in the recruitment, remodeling, and exploitation of neural circuits that support tumor initiation, progression, metastasis, immune evasion, and resistance to therapy. Emerging work in cancer neuroscience has therefore shifted the field from a neuron-centric perspective toward an integrated model of the tumor microenvironment in which malignant cells help establish pathogenic neural niches. This review adopts a tumor-centric perspective to examine how cancer cells drive neoneurogenesis, engage in perineural invasion, and co-opt neural signaling and neuro-immune crosstalk to promote disease progression. It first distinguishes tumor-induced nerve growth and remodeling from perineural invasion as related but mechanistically distinct processes, then considers how tumor cell plasticity and neural mimicry enable malignant cells to acquire neuronal-like traits and exploit neural pathways. The review further explores how tumor-driven innervation shapes angiogenesis, immune modulation, therapeutic resistance, and minimal residual disease while also assessing emerging strategies designed to therapeutically target the tumor-nerve axis. By integrating these themes, the review highlights innervation not as a secondary feature of cancer, but as an active and potentially actionable dimension of tumor biology.

title: Dissecting the Extracellular Vesicle Protein Corona: Proteomic Challenges and Opportunities for Understanding EV Biology and Function.
abstract: Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) are lipid bilayer nanoparticles released by all cell types. They are increasingly studied as sources of molecular information for diagnostics, biomarker discovery, and therapeutic applications. When EVs come into contact with biofluids, they rapidly acquire a layer of adsorbed molecules, known as the biomolecular corona, which consists mainly of proteins. This protein corona can mask or remodel the native EV surface, influence biological interactions, and alter the protein profiles detected by mass spectrometry-based proteomics. As a result, some molecular signatures attributed to EVs may derive from the corona rather than from the vesicles themselves. This is an important source of variability in EV proteomic studies and can affect biomarker interpretation and therapeutic development. Conversely, the protein corona may itself contain biologically relevant information, because it reflects how EVs interact with their physiological or pathological environment. This review summarizes recent advances in EV protein corona research, the main proteomic approaches used for its characterization, and its relevance to EV biology, diagnostics, biomarker discovery, and therapeutic applications.

title: Neural Control Loops in Cancer: From Central Circuits to Local Tumor-Nerve-Immune Ecosystems.
abstract: Cancer is increasingly recognized as an innervated, electrically responsive disease governed by bidirectional interactions between tumors and the nervous system. Within peripheral tumors, autonomic and sensory fibers release neurotransmitters and neuropeptides, while cancer, stromal, immune, and Schwann cells remodel nerves through trophic, guidance, and inflammatory signals. In the central nervous system (CNS), neuronal activity supports glioma growth through activity-dependent mitogens and functional synapses. At the organismal level, stress, inflammation, cachexia, and treatment toxicity engage brain-body circuits that reshape tumor metabolism and immunity. This review organizes these interactions into five modules: central circuit control, autonomic efferents, sensory and nociceptive signaling, neuron-glioma synapses, and local nerve-Schwann-stromal-immune ecosystems. We distinguish human evidence from causal animal and cell model findings, examine perineural invasion as an active multicellular program, and explain context-dependent adrenergic and cholinergic effects. We further assess therapeutic opportunities, including receptor-selective neuromodulation, blockade of trophic and neuroimmune pathways, and combinations with immunotherapy or cytotoxic treatment. Translation will require spatially resolved human validation, longitudinal measures of neural activity, and interventions that preserve essential neural function.

title: KIAA1217 in Human Disease: Emerging Evidence from Fusion Biology, Molecular Mechanisms, and Translational Perspectives.
abstract: KIAA1217, also known as SKT or ETL4, was originally identified as a large, poorly characterized protein-coding gene and is increasingly implicated in human disease. Evidence is most developed in cancer, where KIAA1217 participates in fusions involving RET, FGFR2, and ALK. KIAA1217::RET has direct functional support in lung adenocarcinoma, activating ERK and PI3K/AKT signaling, whereas other fusions are supported mainly by sequencing and case-based observations. Independently, one experimental study indicated that KIAA1217 promotes hepatocellular carcinoma metastasis through JAK1/2-STAT3 signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Studies also implicate KIAA1217 in alternative splicing and multi-omics alterations, although these remain less mechanistically resolved. Beyond cancer, human genetic studies associate KIAA1217 with lumbar disc herniation and vertebral malformations. Experimental evidence for intervertebral disc development and synaptic organization derives primarily from murine Skt models and does not by itself establish equivalent functions of human KIAA1217. Other human and cross-species associations remain exploratory. This review integrates these findings using a multidimensional evidence framework and highlights unresolved links between KIAA1217 structural complexity and tissue-specific functions. Defining its interactome, disease-relevant isoforms, fusion-specific functions, and functional variants will be necessary to clarify KIAA1217-specific mechanisms and determine whether any of these findings have reproducible translational relevance.

title: Beyond ICANS: Cellular and Molecular Mechanisms Linking CAR T-Cell Therapy to Long-Term Neurocognitive Outcomes.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy can cause acute immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), but its delayed neurological and long-term cognitive effects remain incompletely understood. Existing reviews primarily address clinical syndromes or cognitive assessment. This narrative review provides a cross-timescale synthesis of preclinical, neuropathological, biomarker, imaging, and longitudinal clinical evidence linking systemic immune activation, neurovascular interfaces, and central nervous system (CNS) cellular responses. Human studies associate acute ICANS with endothelial and barrier dysfunction, compartmentalized inflammation, and selected astroglial or neuroaxonal injury markers. Persistent microglial reactivity, oligodendroglial alterations, and impaired neurogenesis have predominantly been demonstrated in mice; related human transcriptomic observations derive from CNS-tumor tissue and do not establish persistent injury in hematological CAR T-cell recipients. Prospective clinical cohorts show heterogeneous, often recovering cognitive trajectories rather than uniform long-term deterioration. Acute ICANS, delayed non-ICANSs, and longer-term cognitive outcomes are clinically distinguishable, although their biological separation remains incompletely established. Available treatment studies address predominantly acute toxicity and do not demonstrate prevention of persistent cognitive impairment. We propose testable neurovascular-to-glial and neuronal pathways and a baseline-anchored, multimodal longitudinal framework to connect biological responses and recovery with domain-specific cognitive outcomes.

title: Ischemia-Reperfusion Alters Retrotransposon Transcript Abundance in the Mouse Brain and Acidosis Conditions Are Associated with Transcript Changes in Neuro-2a Cells.
abstract: Retrotransposons are repetitive DNA elements that are normally suppressed through epigenetic mechanisms. In aging and neurodegenerative diseases, abnormal retrotransposon activation occurs and can worsen neurotoxicity. However, it remains unclear whether ischemic stroke induces changes in retrotransposon transcript levels between infarct and peri-infarct brain tissue and whether the abundance of retrotransposon transcripts differs between these regions. To answer this question, we performed 45 min of transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) followed by reperfusion on adult wild-type male mice, then measured expression of retrotransposons LINE-1, IAP and SINE B2 in infarct and peri-infarct brain tissues using RT-qPCR. Next, we performed Western blotting to determine retroviral GAG protein expression. Since brain ischemia leads to tissue acidosis, which exhibits a positive correlation with ischemic brain injury, we further asked whether acidosis itself alters retrotransposon expression. We exposed neuro-2a (N2A) cells to acidic extracellular pH (6.4 or 6.0) and analyzed retrotransposon transcript levels. tMCAO significantly increased transcript abundance of LINE-1 Orf1, IAPEz-gag, IAPEY4 and B2 in ipsilateral ischemic brain tissue compared with sham controls at 24 h. Following correction of the four paired regional comparisons, only the difference in IAPEz-gag expression between infarct and corresponding contralateral region remained statistically significant. Western blotting analysis revealed changes in the abundance and patterns of GAG-immunoreactive proteins, including decreased precursor Pr65 abundance at 6 h of reperfusion, and reduced levels of both Pr65 and mature capsid p30 products at 24 h. In N2A cells, extracellular acidosis was associated with time-dependent increases in the abundance of LINE-1 Orf1, IAPEz-gag and B2 transcripts. Increased cellular injury was also observed under these conditions and may have contributed to these changes. These data suggest distinct retrotransposon transcript profiles between infarct and peri-infarct regions following focal ischemia-reperfusion. Although the in vitro results do not establish whether the transcript changes are attributable to extracellular acidosis, associated cellular injury, or both, exposure to acidic conditions was associated with a subset of the retrotransposon transcript changes observed in ischemic brain tissue. These findings provide a foundation for further investigation of retrotransposon dysregulation in stroke pathology.

title: Cell-Type-Specific Synthesis and Localization of Lactoferrin in the Brain of an APP/PS1 Mouse Model of Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract: Lactoferrin is present in brain cells and is known to protect against injury through anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory processes. Furthermore, it has also been found within amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's disease (AD), leading to the hypothesis that its presence in the AD brain may be detrimental. However, the identity of the brain cells that produce lactoferrin and how its expression changes in AD remain unclear. In this study, we examined lactoferrin expression and localization in 3- and 12-month-old male and female APP/PS1 mice. Using a microglial enrichment protocol and confocal imaging, we identified microglia as an important source of brain lactoferrin, and demonstrated that its expression is modulated by age, sex, and amyloid burden. In female mice, microglial lactoferrin expression was increased at both the mRNA and protein levels in 3-month-old APP/PS1 mice compared with age-matched wild-type controls. Conversely, lactoferrin transcript in the enrichment fraction, and protein localization were also reduced in microglia from 12-month-old female APP/PS1 mice, coinciding with increased amyloid burden. We further demonstrated that gene expression of lactoferrin follows daily variations under a light-dark cycle, similar to established microglial markers such as Iba1 and P2ry12, with alterations in this rhythmic pattern in APP/PS1 mice occurring predominantly in females. In addition, our findings suggest that neurons may internalize lactoferrin via LRP1, whose expression is downregulated by amyloid burden. This Aβ-dependent relationship was further corroborated in both microglial and neuronal in vitro models. Collectively, these findings identify microglia as an important source of lactoferrin in the brain. We suggest that sex- and age-dependent alterations in microglial lactoferrin expression may contribute to the sexual dimorphism observed in AD, possibly through alterations in LRP1-mediated neuronal uptake.

title: DIAPH3 Loss Enhances Chemoresistance in MGMT-Methylated Glioblastoma Cells Through FGFR2 Upregulation.
abstract: Mitotic errors and aneuploidy cause genomic alterations and generate karyotypes that provide tumor cells with growth and survival advantages, enabling them to resist genotoxic insults. Glioblastoma (GBM) tumors are characterized by a high degree of aneuploidy, resistance to therapy, and frequent recurrence, emphasizing the need for additional targetable molecules that can circumvent resistance to standard-of-care strategies and advance therapy. In this paper, we identify DIAPH3 loss as a driver of resistance to Temozolomide (TMZ) and demonstrate its key role in survival of GBM cells. By depleting DIAPH3 expression, we describe how chromosomal instability drives an atypical DNA damage response (DDR) and adaptive mechanisms that collectively support TMZ resistance while blunting apoptosis and evading cell cycle checkpoints. Transcriptomic profiling of DIAPH3-deficient cells further revealed upregulation of Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor 2 (FGFR2), previously linked to DNA repair and radioresistance in glioma, and whose knockdown significantly reduced cell survival under TMZ pressure, establishing FGFR2 as a driver of resistance to therapy in GBM cells. Our findings emphasize a mechanistic link between mitotic fidelity, chromosomal instability, and chemotherapy resistance and may have important clinical implications for understanding and treating glioblastoma. We identify DIAPH3 as a prognostic factor and promising therapeutic target specifically in GBM patients harboring a methylated MGMT promoter; the population most likely to benefit from TMZ treatment. Monitoring DIAPH3 and FGFR2 expression levels may help predict therapy resistance and improve the treatment outcome for MGMT-methylated glioblastoma patients.

title: Acoustic Fault Diagnosis in UAV Propulsion Systems Using GA-Optimized Bio-Inspired Liquid Neural Networks.
abstract: Biologically inspired neural computation offers a promising approach to processing complex temporal signals in autonomous engineering systems. However, acoustic fault diagnosis remains challenging under non-stationary operating conditions, particularly when multiple motors operate simultaneously and produce overlapping acoustic patterns that complicate fault identification. This study investigates a biologically inspired Liquid Neural Network (LNN) framework integrating heterogeneous Izhikevich spiking neurons, Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP), and Genetic Algorithm (GA)-based neuronal parameter optimization. The proposed architecture combines locally adapted recurrent synaptic connections with evolutionarily selected neuronal parameters to support fault-related temporal representation. Acoustic recordings representing healthy operation and four propulsion fault conditions were divided into 1500 non-overlapping one-second segments. Log-Mel acoustic representations and complementary descriptors were processed using a 64-neuron spiking reservoir and a regularized Ridge readout. Performance was evaluated using temporally blocked data partitions and a retrospective test subset of 290 segments across five random seeds. The proposed GA-STDP-LNN achieved an accuracy of 93.59 ± 0.87%, a macro F1 score of 93.60 ± 0.87%, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.9214 ± 0.0107. Under synthetic noise, macro F1 decreased to 83.87% at 20 dB and 6.67% at 10 dB. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining biologically inspired neuronal dynamics, synaptic plasticity, and evolutionary optimization for acoustic fault classification, while highlighting the need for independent recording-based validation and improved robustness under severe acoustic disturbances.

title: Connectomes as Structural Priors for Embodied Control: Lessons from Digital Drosophila.
abstract: Synapse-resolved connectomes of Drosophila melanogaster now map the entire adult brain and ventral nerve cord, but behavior also depends on synaptic strengths, neural dynamics, and the body. A connectome is therefore better used as a testable structural prior than as a blueprint to copy. This review examines how digital Drosophila (connectomes plus the models and body simulators built on them) can serve this role in embodied control. We trace how electron-microscopy images become a connectivity graph, where errors enter, and how heterogeneous datasets can be combined reproducibly. We then compare three uses of the graph (extracting a circuit principle, embedding a reconstructed module, or adopting the whole connectome as controller topology) with one another and with conventional controllers, separating experimentally validated findings from computational predictions. Connectome-constrained models can predict neural activity and sensorimotor pathways, but simulated success does not by itself establish biological accuracy, and sensory encoding, motor decoding, and body mechanics are as much part of the controller as the wiring. From this synthesis we derive five candidate design principles (sparse modular communication, recurrent state estimation, hierarchical motor control, selective plasticity, and body-controller co-design) and one methodological principle (anatomically indexed intervention), each paired with falsifiable predictions, matched baselines, and sim-to-real stress tests.
